rv.q: Under the layered direction of Margot Bordelon, the ensemble is as good as it gets in bringing Spector's characters to life and the humor in his writing to full bloom.

The above scene will seem all-too familiar to anyone well-acquainted with social media platforms but it is the impeccable timing between the actors' dialogue and the projected imagery that really makes the entire scene work.
Tension builds, friendships are tested and chaos most assuredly ensues while remaining thoroughly funny and compelling.
When I recommend this production to others, and I do, this scene is the one I have most in mind.
You may perceive it differently if you see 'Eureka Day.' Which you should.

The rest of the play may feel a bit dated, circular, and unnuanced at times, but there is no denying that Spector has written a play that both plumbs the limits of honest, benevolent, open-mindedness and allows us to recognize and poke fun at ourselves.
This is a well-shaped and paced production that is equally as well-proportioned by the design staff and acted by its cast.
